prompt.spicy: Six stuck moments. Name the gap in each one — because the gap decides whether it's your problem or theirs.
prompt.boardroom: Six blockages. Identify the gap in each, since the type of gap determines whether it is yours to resolve or theirs.

label.spicy: "Can you look at the churn numbers" — you don't know if they want a chart, a view, or a recommendation
label.boardroom: "Can you review the churn figures" — it is unclear whether a chart, an assessment or a recommendation is expected

reason.spicy: You don't know what done looks like. Nobody can work that out from the file — it's a thirty-second answer that only exists in their head, so it's a fair thing to ask.
reason.boardroom: The definition of completion is unknown and cannot be derived from the material. It is held only by the requester, so asking is appropriate.

label.spicy: You need to combine two datasets and you've never used a lookup formula
label.boardroom: You need to merge two datasets and have not previously used a lookup function

reason.spicy: Findable in ten minutes by anyone, including you. Asking a colleague to teach you this is spending their time on something the internet does for free and faster.
reason.boardroom: This is resolvable independently within minutes. Requesting instruction spends a colleague's time on something readily available elsewhere.

label.spicy: The deck needs sign-off before it leaves the building and you don't know who signs
label.boardroom: The document requires approval before external release and the approver is unknown

reason.spicy: A rule exists and you can't see it. Look for it once — old email threads, the wiki — then ask precisely: "who signs off client-facing decks, is it Dani or does it need legal?"
reason.boardroom: A rule exists but is not visible to you. Search once — previous correspondence, internal documentation — then ask precisely who approves client-facing material.

label.spicy: Two defensible ways to present a bad result. One protects the relationship, one is more transparent
label.boardroom: Two defensible presentations of an unfavourable result: one protects the relationship, one is more transparent

reason.spicy: This is the one people sit on. You don't have the authority or the client history to pick — and if you pick silently and it's the wrong call, the silence is the part that gets remembered.
reason.boardroom: This is frequently left unresolved. You hold neither the authority nor the client history to choose, and an unflagged choice is the element that will be scrutinised later.

label.spicy: The export keeps failing with an error code you've never seen
label.boardroom: The export fails with an unfamiliar error code

reason.spicy: Paste the exact error into search first. If it's still failing after ten minutes, it upgrades — you then ask with the error text and what you already ruled out.
reason.boardroom: Search the exact error text first. If unresolved after ten minutes, escalate with the error text and the steps already eliminated.

label.spicy: You genuinely don't understand what the client's business does, and you're writing their strategy summary
label.boardroom: You do not understand the client's business model and are drafting their strategy summary

reason.spicy: Not a method gap and not a clarification. You can't judge whether your own output is right, which means this is a scope conversation — say so now, in plain words, rather than producing something confident and hollow.
reason.boardroom: This is neither a method gap nor a clarification. You cannot evaluate your own output, which makes it a scope conversation. Raise it directly rather than producing confident but unfounded work.

verdict.spicy: Two were yours to solve, two were theirs, one was a rule you could half-find, and one wasn't a question at all. Most people over-ask on method and under-ask on decisions.
verdict.boardroom: Two were yours to resolve, two were theirs, one was a partially documented rule, and one was not a question at all. The common pattern is over-asking on method and under-asking on decisions.

principle.spicy: Name the gap before you open your mouth. Method is yours. Decisions are theirs. Goal is cheap to ask and expensive to guess.
principle.boardroom: Identify the gap before asking. Method is yours; decisions are theirs; the goal is inexpensive to confirm and costly to assume.

prompt.spicy:
Same gap, five ways of asking. You're mid-way through a competitor analysis and you've realised the brief says "top five competitors" but the client's own deck lists eight, three of which are in a different market.

Which message do you send?
prompt.boardroom:
One gap, five phrasings. You are part-way through a competitor analysis and have noticed the brief specifies the top five competitors while the client's own material lists eight, three of which operate in a different market.

Which message do you send?

label.spicy: "Brief says top five, client's deck lists eight — three of those are in adjacent markets so I've read the five as UK-market only, which is the comparison that makes their positioning argument work. Building it that way; shout if you meant all eight."
label.boardroom: "The brief specifies five competitors; the client's material lists eight, three of which operate in adjacent markets. I have interpreted the five as UK-market only, which supports their positioning argument, and am proceeding on that basis unless you intended all eight."

consequence.spicy: You spotted the discrepancy, worked out *why* it exists, made the call the analysis needs, and gave them a one-word exit. This is what senior looks like in writing.
consequence.boardroom: You identified the inconsistency, established its likely cause, made the judgement the analysis requires, and left a single-word correction available. This reads as experienced.

label.spicy: "Brief says five competitors, their deck says eight — which do you want me to use?"
label.boardroom: "The brief specifies five competitors and the client's material lists eight. Which should I use?"

consequence.spicy: Genuinely fine. You caught a real inconsistency and asked precisely. It just hands the thinking back — you'd noticed the market difference and didn't say so.
consequence.boardroom: Perfectly acceptable. You identified a real inconsistency and asked precisely, but returned the analysis to them without noting the market distinction you had already observed.

label.spicy: "Just to check — are we doing five or eight?"
label.boardroom: "To confirm, is this five or eight?"

consequence.spicy: Answerable, but stripped of everything you know. They can't tell whether you've read the client deck or just counted rows, so they'll re-explain the brief to you.
consequence.boardroom: Answerable, but conveys none of your analysis. It is unclear whether you have read the client material, so the brief will likely be re-explained to you.

label.spicy: "Sorry to bother you! Really stupid question but I'm a bit confused about the competitor bit — no rush at all!"
label.boardroom: "Apologies for the interruption — a minor question about the competitor section, whenever convenient."

consequence.spicy: Three apologies, no question. They now have to extract the actual issue from you, which costs more of their time than the thing you were trying not to cost them.
consequence.boardroom: Apologetic framing with no stated question. The issue must now be drawn out of you, which consumes more of their time than a direct question would have.

label.spicy: Say nothing, use five, and mention the discrepancy in the meeting if it comes up
label.boardroom: Say nothing, proceed with five, and raise the discrepancy in the meeting if relevant

consequence.spicy: You found a flaw in the brief and sat on it. If the client asks about the missing three in the room, the person presenting finds out at the same time they do.
consequence.boardroom: You identified a flaw in the brief and withheld it. If the client raises the omitted three in the meeting, the presenter learns of it at the same moment they do.

verdict.spicy: The gap between B and A is not politeness or length. It's whether you transmitted the thinking you'd already done — you'd noticed the adjacent markets either way.
verdict.boardroom: The distinction between B and A is not tone or length. It is whether the analysis you had already completed was transmitted; the market observation existed in both cases.

principle.spicy: State your working, your assumption, its cost, and what you'll do by default. Four lines. It reads as authority and it's mostly just admin.
principle.boardroom: State your working, your assumption, its consequence, and your default action. Four lines, which read as authority and are largely procedural.

prompt.spicy: You've hit a method gap at 10am. Put these in the order you should actually do them — the whole thing should take under fifteen minutes.
prompt.boardroom: You encounter a method gap at 10am. Place these in the order they should be carried out; the sequence should take under fifteen minutes.

label.spicy: Search the exact error text or the exact phrase from the brief
label.boardroom: Search the exact error text or the precise wording of the brief

label.spicy: Open the last version of this work someone else did and see how they handled it
label.boardroom: Review the most recent comparable work and how it was handled

label.spicy: Write one sentence: what you're trying to do, and the exact point it breaks
label.boardroom: Write one sentence stating the objective and the precise point of failure

label.spicy: Add what you've already ruled out, and what you'll do by default if nobody replies
label.boardroom: Add the options already eliminated and the default action if there is no response

label.spicy: Send it to the one person most likely to know — not the channel, not your manager by reflex
label.boardroom: Send it to the individual most likely to know, rather than a channel or your manager by default

verdict.spicy: Search, copy, write the sentence, add the default, send it to one person. Step three ends it surprisingly often — writing "it breaks when I…" is where you find out you already knew.
verdict.boardroom: Search, model, articulate, state a default, send to one person. The third step frequently resolves the issue: articulating the failure point often reveals the answer.

principle.spicy: Ten minutes of looking, then ask with the looking attached. The attachment is what makes it a good question rather than a fast one.
principle.boardroom: Ten minutes of investigation, then ask and include what you found. The inclusion is what distinguishes a good question from a quick one.

prompt.spicy: Swipe. Fast. The considered answer lands after each one.
prompt.boardroom: Respond quickly. The considered answer follows each statement.

statement.spicy: You should batch your questions rather than sending them as they occur to you.
statement.boardroom: Questions should be consolidated rather than sent individually as they arise.

nuance.spicy: Three questions in one message costs someone one context switch. The same three across a morning costs three, and the research on interruption says the damage outlasts the interruption itself. The exception is anything that blocks you completely or gets more expensive by the hour — those go immediately.
nuance.boardroom: Three questions in a single message require one context switch; the same three spread across a morning require three, and the disruption extends beyond the interruption itself. The exception is anything fully blocking or increasing in cost over time, which should be raised immediately.

statement.spicy: If you preface a question with "sorry, this is probably a stupid question", you're being appropriately humble.
statement.boardroom: Prefacing a question with an apology demonstrates appropriate humility.

nuance.spicy: You're pre-loading their judgement for them. They hadn't decided it was stupid until you offered. Humility is showing your working and being genuinely open to being wrong — it isn't a disclaimer at the top of a message.
nuance.boardroom: The framing supplies an assessment they had not yet formed. Humility is demonstrated by showing your reasoning and remaining open to correction, not by a disclaimer preceding the question.

statement.spicy: Asking your manager the same thing twice is worse than getting it wrong.
statement.boardroom: Asking a manager the same question twice is worse than proceeding incorrectly.

nuance.spicy: Getting it wrong is nearly always worse, and this fear produces a lot of quietly incorrect work. The actual fix is upstream: write the answer down the first time. Repeat questions aren't a memory failure, they're a note-taking one.
nuance.boardroom: Proceeding incorrectly is almost always more costly, and this concern produces a considerable amount of quietly inaccurate work. The remedy is to record the answer the first time; repeated questions reflect record-keeping rather than memory.

statement.spicy: There's a point where you should say you don't understand the work well enough to be doing it.
statement.boardroom: There is a threshold at which you should state that you do not understand the work well enough to undertake it.

nuance.spicy: And the test is specific: can you say in one sentence what this is for and who is harmed if it's wrong? If not, more clarifying questions won't save it — that's a scope conversation and it's cheap on Monday and career-shaped on Thursday.
nuance.boardroom: The test is specific: can you state in one sentence what the work is for and who is affected if it is incorrect? If not, further clarification will not resolve it. That is a scope conversation, and its cost rises sharply with delay.

statement.spicy: Senior people ask fewer questions than junior people.
statement.boardroom: Senior colleagues ask fewer questions than junior ones.

nuance.spicy: Watch one for a week. They ask constantly — they just ask about goals, constraints and decisions rather than method, and they arrive with a position attached. Volume isn't the variable. Type is.
nuance.boardroom: Observation suggests otherwise. Senior colleagues ask frequently, but about goals, constraints and decisions rather than method, and they arrive with a proposed position. The variable is type, not volume.

statement.spicy: "Any update on this?" is a reasonable follow-up message.
statement.boardroom: "Any update on this?" is a reasonable follow-up.

nuance.spicy: It transfers the whole job of remembering to them. "Still planning to send the pack at 3 — going with the standard discount unless I hear otherwise" does the same chase, requires nothing from them, and moves the work whether they answer or not.
nuance.boardroom: It transfers the burden of recollection entirely to them. A follow-up stating your intended action and default achieves the same prompt, requires no response, and allows the work to continue regardless.

verdict.spicy: The thread: good asking is about type and structure, not volume or apology. Nobody has ever been marked down for a question that arrived with a position attached.
verdict.boardroom: The common thread: effective asking is a matter of type and structure rather than frequency or tone. A question accompanied by a proposed position is rarely received poorly.

principle.spicy: Batch it, drop the apology, bring a default, and know the line where a question becomes a scope conversation.
principle.boardroom: Consolidate, remove the apology, propose a default, and recognise the point at which a question becomes a scope conversation.
